column9: Which statement best defines an **isotope**?
column14: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
column15: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number
column16: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of protons
column17: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of electrons
column28: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, so the atomic number stays the same and the mass number changes. Changing protons makes a different element, and changing electrons makes an ion, not an isotope.
column29: Which particle can change without changing which element the atom is?

column9: Two different isotopes of the same element always have the same ___.
column28: Isotopes of one element always have the same number of protons (the same atomic number). Their neutrons are different, so their mass numbers and masses are different too.
column29: What particle gives an atom its identity?

column9: Isotopes of the same element have different numbers of protons.
column28: False. Isotopes have the same number of protons; the number of neutrons is what differs. An atom with a different number of protons is a different element.
column29: If the number of protons changed, would it still be the same element?

column9: In hyphen notation such as potassium-40, the number after the dash is the ___ number.
column28: Hyphen notation is element name – mass number. In potassium-40, 40 is the mass number (protons + neutrons). It is not the atomic number, which is 19 for potassium.
column29: Is 40 the number of protons alone, or protons plus neutrons?

column9: In the nuclear notation $^{40}_{19}\text{K}$, what does the top number, 40, stand for?
column28: The top number is the mass number, protons plus neutrons. The bottom number, 19, is the atomic number. The number of neutrons is not written; you find it by subtracting the bottom number from the top number.
column29: The top number counts the particles in the nucleus that each have a mass of 1 amu.

column9: In nuclear notation like $^{14}_{6}\text{C}$, what does the bottom number tell you?
column28: The bottom number is the atomic number (number of protons). For carbon it is 6. The top number, 14, is the mass number.
column29: Which number is the same for every atom of carbon?

column9: An unstable nucleus results from too many or too few ___.
column28: Neutrons hold the nucleus together, so an unstable nucleus results from too many or too few neutrons. Changing protons would change the element.
column29: Which particle holds the nucleus together and is the one that differs between isotopes?

column9: Match each term to its meaning.
column14: Isotope :: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
column15: Mass number :: Number of protons plus neutrons
column17: Average atomic mass :: Weighted average of all of an element's isotopes
column28: An isotope differs in neutrons; mass number = protons + neutrons; atomic number = protons; average atomic mass is the weighted average of all the isotopes (the decimal number on the periodic table).
column29: Mass number is a whole number for one isotope. Average atomic mass is a decimal for the whole element.

column9: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 have the same number of protons.
column28: True. Both are carbon, so both have 6 protons. They have different numbers of neutrons, and that is why their mass numbers are different.
column29: Are they both still carbon?

column9: Carbon-12, carbon-13, and carbon-14 are all isotopes of carbon. Which particle do they have different numbers of?
column28: They are all carbon, so each has 6 protons (and 6 electrons when neutral). Only the number of neutrons changes, which is why the mass numbers are 12, 13, and 14.
column29: What is the only particle that can change while the atom stays carbon and stays neutral?

column9: Which pair of atoms are isotopes of the same element?
column28: Hydrogen-1 and hydrogen-2 are both hydrogen (1 proton) with different mass numbers, so they have different numbers of neutrons. The other pairs are different elements, even when the mass number matches.
column29: Isotopes must be the same element. Look at the names first.

column9: Atoms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons are called ___.
column28: These are isotopes. Same element = same protons; different neutrons = different mass numbers.
column29: It is the vocabulary word for this whole learning target.

column9: According to the class notes, when is an isotope's nucleus most stable?
column14: When it has more electrons than protons
column15: When the mass number is as large as possible
column16: When the number of protons and neutrons are the same
column17: When it has no neutrons at all
column28: The notes say an isotope is most stable when the number of p⁺ and n⁰ are the same. Electrons are outside the nucleus, and neutrons are needed to hold the nucleus together.
column29: Stability is about the nucleus. Which two particles are in the nucleus?

column9: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 react the same way in chemical reactions. Why?
column14: They have the same number of neutrons
column15: They have the same mass number
column17: They have the same number of electrons
column28: Electrons control how an atom reacts, and both isotopes have 6 electrons (and 6 protons). Their neutrons, mass numbers, and masses are different, so those cannot be the reason.
column29: Which particle is in charge of reactivity?

column9: The mass number of each isotope is printed on the periodic table.
column28: False. The mass number is not on the periodic table. The table shows the average atomic mass, a decimal that is a weighted average of all of the element's isotopes.
column29: Is the mass number on the periodic table a whole number or a decimal?

column9: Potassium has atomic number 19. How many neutrons are in one atom of potassium-40?
column28: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 40 − 19 = 21. The 40 in potassium-40 is the mass number.
column29: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Which number is the mass number in potassium-40?

column9: How many neutrons are in one atom of $^{18}_{8}\text{O}$?
column28: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 18 − 8 = 10. The top number is the mass number and the bottom number is the atomic number.
column29: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Top number minus bottom number.

column9: Carbon has atomic number 6. How many neutrons are in one atom of carbon-14?
column28: Neutrons = 14 − 6 = 8. A common mistake is answering 14, which is the mass number (protons + neutrons).
column29: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

column9: A neutral atom has a mass number of 37 and 20 neutrons. How many electrons does it have?
column28: Protons = mass number − neutrons = 37 − 20 = 17. In a neutral atom, electrons = protons, so it has 17 electrons (it is chlorine-37).
column29: First find the protons: mass number = protons + neutrons. Then use the neutral-atom rule.

column9: An isotope of magnesium (Mg, atomic number 12) has 14 neutrons. What is its mass number?
column28: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 12 + 14 = 26, so it is magnesium-26.
column29: Mass number = protons + neutrons. How many protons does every magnesium atom have?

column9: An isotope of sodium (Na, atomic number 11) has 13 neutrons. What number goes on top when you write it in nuclear notation?
column28: The top number is the mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 13 = 24. The isotope is $^{24}_{11}\text{Na}$, sodium-24.
column29: The top number in nuclear notation is the mass number, not the neutrons.

column9: Iron (Fe) has atomic number 26. Which is the correct nuclear notation for iron-58?
column28: Mass number (58) goes on top and atomic number (26) goes on the bottom: $^{58}_{26}\text{Fe}$. 32 is the number of neutrons (58 − 26), which is not written in the notation.
column29: Top = mass number (the number in the hyphen name). Bottom = atomic number.

column9: An atom has 8 protons and 9 neutrons. Element 8 is oxygen. What is its hyphen notation?
column28: 8 protons makes it oxygen. Mass number = 8 + 9 = 17, so it is oxygen-17. The 9 neutrons do not change the element, so it is not fluorine.
column29: Hyphen notation = element name – mass number. Mass number = protons + neutrons.

column9: Nitrogen has the symbol N. The hyphen notation for $^{15}_{7}\text{N}$ is ___.
column28: Hyphen notation = element name – mass number. The top number, 15, is the mass number, so $^{15}_{7}\text{N}$ is nitrogen-15. The 7 is the atomic number and is not part of the hyphen name.
column29: Write the element's name, a dash, then the top number.

column9: Boron has two natural isotopes, boron-10 and boron-11. Boron's average atomic mass is 10.81. Which isotope is more common?
column15: They are equally common, since there are only two
column17: You cannot tell without counting the atoms
column28: The average atomic mass is closest to the mass number of the most common isotope. 10.81 is closer to 11 than to 10, so most boron atoms are boron-11. If they were equally common, the average would be 10.5.
column29: Is 10.81 closer to 10 or to 11? The average gets pulled toward the isotope there is more of.

column9: Lithium's average atomic mass is 6.94. What is the mass number of lithium's most common isotope?
column28: Round the average atomic mass to the nearest whole number: 6.94 → 7. The most common isotope is lithium-7.
column29: The average atomic mass is closest to the mass number of the most common isotope. Round it.

column9: Compare a neutral atom of carbon-12 with a neutral atom of carbon-13. Which of these are the SAME for both atoms? Select all that apply.
column28: Both are carbon, so they share the number of protons (6), the atomic number (6), the number of electrons (6), and the symbol C. The number of neutrons and the mass numbers (12 vs 13) are different.
column29: Only one particle differs between isotopes. Anything that depends on that particle is different too.

column9: Jae says, “If you change the top number in $^{12}_{6}\text{C}$ to 13, it becomes a different element.” Is Jae right?
column14: Yes. Changing the mass number always changes the element.
column15: Yes. Element 13 is aluminum, so it becomes aluminum.
column16: No. The top number is the number of electrons, so it becomes an ion.
column17: No. The atomic number is still 6, so it is still carbon, just a different isotope.
column28: The top number is the mass number. Changing it from 12 to 13 adds a neutron, which makes $^{13}_{6}\text{C}$, still carbon. Only changing the atomic number (protons) changes the element.
column29: Which number in nuclear notation identifies the element: the top or the bottom?

column9: $^{14}_{6}\text{C}$ and $^{14}_{7}\text{N}$ are isotopes of each other because they have the same mass number.
column28: False. They have different atomic numbers (6 and 7), so they are different elements. Isotopes must have the same atomic number and different mass numbers.
column29: Check the bottom numbers. Are these the same element?

column9: Match each nuclear notation to its hyphen notation.
column28: Hyphen notation = element name – top number. Mg is magnesium, S is sulfur, Ca is calcium, and N is nitrogen. The bottom number is the atomic number and is left out of the hyphen name.
column29: Use the element's name and the top (mass) number, not the bottom number.

column9: Put these isotopes in order from the FEWEST neutrons to the MOST neutrons.
column29: Find the neutrons for each one first: mass number − atomic number. Do not sort by the top number.

column9: Put the steps in order to find the number of neutrons in the most common isotope of aluminum when you only have a periodic table.
column14: Subtract the atomic number from the mass number
column15: Find aluminum's box on the periodic table
column16: Round the average atomic mass to the nearest whole number
column28: Find aluminum's box, read the average atomic mass (26.982), round it to get the mass number (27), then subtract the atomic number: 27 − 13 = 14 neutrons.
column29: You need a mass number before you can subtract. Where does the mass number come from when none is given?

column9: How many protons, neutrons, and electrons are in a neutral atom of $^{39}_{19}\text{K}$?
column28: Protons = atomic number = 19. Neutrons = 39 − 19 = 20. Electrons = protons = 19 in a neutral atom.
column29: p⁺ = bottom number, n⁰ = top − bottom, e⁻ = p⁺ if neutral.

column9: Which two atoms are isotopes of the same element?
column28: Isotopes have the same bottom number (atomic number) and different top numbers (mass numbers). Both neon atoms have 10 protons but 10 and 12 neutrons. The other pairs have different atomic numbers, so they are different elements.
column29: Compare the bottom numbers first. They must match.

column9: The mass of the most common isotope of an element is known based on the element's ___ (the decimal number on the periodic table).
column20: average atomic mass|atomic mass|average mass|avg atomic mass
column28: The average atomic mass is closest to the mass number of the most common isotope, so rounding it tells you the most common isotope.
column29: It is a weighted average of all the isotopes.

column9: How many MORE neutrons does $^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}$ have than $^{40}_{20}\text{Ca}$?
column28: Fe: 56 − 26 = 30 neutrons. Ca: 40 − 20 = 20 neutrons. Difference = 30 − 20 = 10. A common mistake is 56 − 40 = 16, which compares mass numbers, not neutrons.
column29: Find the neutrons in each atom first (mass number − atomic number), then subtract.

column9: An isotope of fluorine (atomic number 9) has the same number of neutrons as $^{20}_{10}\text{Ne}$. What is the mass number of this fluorine isotope?
column28: Neutrons in Ne-20 = 20 − 10 = 10. Fluorine mass number = 9 + 10 = 19, so it is fluorine-19.
column29: Step 1: neutrons in the neon = mass number − atomic number. Step 2: mass number = protons + neutrons.

column9: Silicon has three natural isotopes: silicon-28, silicon-29, and silicon-30. Silicon's average atomic mass is 28.085. Which isotope is the most common?
column28: The average atomic mass is closest to the most common isotope. 28.085 is very close to 28, so silicon-28 is the most common. If all three were equally common, the average would be 29.
column29: Which mass number is the average closest to?

column9: Argon has three natural isotopes: argon-36, argon-38, and argon-40. Argon's average atomic mass is 39.948. Which statement is best supported?
column14: Most argon atoms are argon-38, because it is in the middle.
column15: All three isotopes are equally common, so the average is 38.
column16: Most argon atoms are argon-36, because lighter isotopes are more common.
column28: 39.948 rounds to 40, and the average atomic mass is closest to the mass number of the most common isotope, so most argon is argon-40. An equal mix would average 38.
column29: Round the average atomic mass. Which isotope's mass number does it match?

column9: Which nuclear notation is written incorrectly?
column28: In $^{6}_{12}\text{C}$ the numbers are flipped: the atomic number (6) is on top. The mass number must go on top, so it should be $^{12}_{6}\text{C}$. A mass number can never be smaller than the atomic number.
column29: Top = mass number, bottom = atomic number. Which one has a top number smaller than its bottom number?

column9: Atomic numbers: H = 1, C = 6, Na = 11, K = 19. Which nuclear notation does NOT match its element?
column28: Carbon's atomic number is 6, so carbon-14 is $^{14}_{6}\text{C}$. $^{14}_{7}\text{C}$ has the wrong bottom number; 7 protons would be nitrogen, not carbon.
column29: Check each bottom number against the atomic numbers given.

column9: An atom has 12 protons and 13 neutrons. Element 12 is magnesium (Mg). Which are correct ways to write this isotope? Select all that apply.
column28: Mass number = 12 + 13 = 25, so it is magnesium-25 (or Mg-25), $^{25}_{12}\text{Mg}$, or $^{25}\text{Mg}$ (the bottom number can be left off). Magnesium-13 uses the neutrons instead of the mass number, and $^{12}_{25}\text{Mg}$ has the numbers flipped.
column29: Find the mass number first (protons + neutrons). Then check where each form puts it.

column9: Gold (Au) has atomic number 79 and an average atomic mass of 196.97. Gold has only one natural isotope. How many neutrons does it have?
column28: Round the average atomic mass to get the mass number: 196.97 → 197. Neutrons = 197 − 79 = 118.
column29: No mass number is given, so round the average atomic mass first. Then neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

column9: Strontium (Sr) has atomic number 38 and an average atomic mass of 87.62. How many neutrons are in strontium's most common isotope?
column28: 87.62 rounds to 88, the mass number of the most common isotope. Neutrons = 88 − 38 = 50.
column29: Round the average atomic mass to get the mass number, then use mass number − atomic number.

column9: A bar graph shows that less than 1% of zinc atoms are zinc-70. Ava claims, “Zinc-70 must be unstable, because there is so little of it.” Which is the best response?
column14: She is right, because rare isotopes are always unstable.
column15: She is right, because zinc-70 has more protons than other zinc isotopes.
column16: The graph only shows how common each isotope is, not whether it is stable.
column17: She is wrong, because zinc-70 is the most common zinc isotope.
column28: An abundance graph tells how common each isotope is. It says nothing about stability, so the data do not support Ava's claim. All zinc isotopes have the same number of protons, and the graph shows zinc-70 is rare, not most common.
column29: What does the graph actually measure? Does that measurement say anything about stability?

column9: Atom A has 16 protons, 16 neutrons, and 16 electrons. Atom B has 16 protons, 18 neutrons, and 16 electrons. Atoms A and B are isotopes of the same element.
column28: True. Both have 16 protons, so they are the same element (sulfur). They have different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers are different (32 and 34). That is the definition of isotopes.
column29: Compare the protons first, then the neutrons.

column9: Atom X has 20 protons and 22 neutrons. Atom Y has 22 protons and 20 neutrons. Which statement is correct?
column14: They are isotopes, because they have the same mass number.
column15: They are isotopes, because they have the same total number of particles in the nucleus.
column16: They are the same element, because both contain 20 of one particle.
column17: They have the same mass number but are different elements, so they are not isotopes.
column28: Both have mass number 42 (20 + 22), but X has 20 protons (calcium) and Y has 22 protons (titanium). Different protons means different elements, so they cannot be isotopes.
column29: Isotopes need the same number of protons. Do X and Y have the same number of protons?

column9: An isotope of uranium has 3 fewer neutrons than $^{238}_{92}\text{U}$. What is the mass number of this isotope?
column28: Neutrons in U-238 = 238 − 92 = 146. The new isotope has 146 − 3 = 143 neutrons. Mass number = 92 + 143 = 235, so it is uranium-235. The protons stay at 92 because it is still uranium.
column29: Find the neutrons in uranium-238 first. The protons do not change for an isotope.

column9: Match each isotope to the number of neutrons in one atom.
column29: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number for each one.

column9: Carbon has atomic number 6. An isotope of carbon has 7 neutrons. In hyphen notation, this isotope is ___.
column28: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 6 + 7 = 13, so the isotope is carbon-13. Carbon-7 is a common mistake; hyphen notation uses the mass number, not the neutrons.
column29: Hyphen notation uses the mass number. Mass number = protons + neutrons.
